Depending on charging power requirements and local grid characteristics, the costs to procure, install, and use electric vehicle service equipment (EVSE) can range widely. Level 2 EVSE installed in a residence costs on the order of $1,000 per plug, and can typically provide regular charging at a low fixed price.8 In contrast, up-front costs for high-power EVSE for public use or for commercial vehicles can vary more widely, increasing to hundreds of thousands of dollars per plug if substantial electricity infrastructure upgrades are required11,12,13. Further, charging costs can exceed petroleum fueling costs when high-power charging is subject to expensive peak demand prices or experiences low levels of utilization14. To date, these kinds of variability and uncertainty have posed obstacles to assessing and communicating the economics of EV charging, in turn posing an obstacle to the adoption of EVs. Many of the economic, social, technical, and managerial challenges associated with charging infrastructure arise at the interface between the electricity and transportation systems, where physical connections are made and flows of energy, money, and information are negotiated. Charging infrastructure embodies a set of tight temporal and spatial linkages between the two systems. From the electricity system perspective, utilities must equate energy supply and demand at a high resolution in time and space, a task which is made simpler by steady and predictable usage patterns. However, on the transportation side, charging tends to exhibit unsteady and unpredictable usage patterns, particularly in applications of extreme fast charging15. Optimizing to meet the needs of both systems must begin with a comprehensive understanding of those needs and how they interact. Just as a typical electric utility operator is unlikely to be familiar with the detailed requirements of a long-haul freight trucking operation, a typical homeowner or fleet manager is unlikely to understand the imperatives governing electricity rate design. Rather than insisting that operators of either system become an expert in the other, there is potential for a third party to provide communication and optimization services for collective benefit. The set of emerging infrastructure ownership and usage models involving this kind of third party are known as “Charging-as-a-Service” (ChaaS).
